outline.chapter_title: 1. Introduction to RL for Language Models
outline.description: Provide historical context and motivate the need for stable RL algorithms when scaling large language models (LLMs). Explain the role of RL in enabling complex reasoning tasks and introduce the challenges discussed in the paper, including catastrophic collapse in existing methods.
subtopics: Historical evolution of RL in NLP

outline.description: Lay out the essential mathematical framework: policies, queries, responses, rewards, and standard baseline algorithms such as PPO and GRPO. Clarify notation used through the rest of the text.
subtopics: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) objective and importance ratios
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective and advantages

outline.description: Explain the statistical foundation of importance sampling and show how GRPO’s token‑level weighting violates this principle, leading to high‑variance gradients that accumulate over long sequences.
subtopics: Misalignment between reward and gradient units

outline.chapter_title: 4. The Core Idea of GSPO – Sequence‑Level Clipping
outline.description: Introduce the main insight: optimization should operate on the same unit that rewards are assigned to—entire sequences. Discuss why sequence likelihoods are a natural importance ratio and how length‑normalization controls variance.
Derive the GSPO objective, explain its components, and compare it directly to GRPO. Discuss advantages estimation at group level and how clipping operates on whole responses.
subtopics: ε clipping ranges in GSPO vs GRPO

outline.description: Step through the derivation of GSPO’s gradient, contrast it with GRPO’s gradient, and highlight why equal token weighting yields lower variance.
subtopics: Empirical observations on clipped token fractions

outline.description: Present a finer‑grained version that still uses sequence‑level weighting but allows token‑wise advantages for specific use cases such as multi‑turn RL.
Discuss how MoE architectures introduce expert activation volatility and how GSPO naturally mitigates this problem without complex workarounds like Routing Replay.
Explain how GSPO’s tolerance to precision discrepancies between training and inference engines simplifies reinforcement learning pipelines, particularly in distributed or partial rollout scenarios.
subtopics: Training vs inference engine precision issues
Benefits for partial rollout & multi–turn RL

outline.description: Summarize experimental setup (Qwen3–30B base cold start), hyperparameters, comparison metrics (AIME'24 Pass@1, LiveCodeBench Pass@1, CodeForces Elo). Present key results highlighting stability, efficiency, MoE training success, and infrastructure simplification.
subtopics: Clipping range settings for GSPO vs GRPO

outline.chapter_title: 11. Design Principles for Scalable RL Algorithms
outline.description: Abstract lessons learned from GSPI: alignment of reward units with optimization units, proper use of importance sampling at correct granularity, handling huge batch sizes with mini-batches, measurements of clipping effectiveness.
Discuss potential extensions such as adaptive clipping ranges, hybrid sequence/token objectives beyond GLSCO token variant, integration with value models for multi‑objective training.
subtopics: Hybrid objectives combining policy gradients & Q-learning
Scaling to multi‑modal or instruction tuned LLMs
Exploring reward functions beyond binary scores

outline.description: Conclude with a concise recap: GSPI resolves instability by aligning gradients with rewards at sequence level; it improves efficiency; eliminates additional MoE hacking; simplifies infrastructure; underpins Qwen3 success.
